summary: Defines a SIP URI parameter that identifies the inter-operator traffic leg in 3GPP networks. A call path can be split into legs that each cross different operators, and this parameter lets a network indicate which leg a request belongs to.

eli5.summary: A long trip has several stretches run by different bus companies. This label says which stretch a message belongs to.

questions: what is the sip iotl parameter
what is a traffic leg in 3gpp
subtitle: A small SIP URI parameter that labels which stretch of a call's signaling path a request is about to cross.

tldr.problem: In 3GPP networks a call's signaling path is split into traffic legs that can cross different operators, and intermediaries need to know which kind of leg they are handling to apply the right policy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7549 defines the SIP URI parameter 'iotl' (Inter-Operator Traffic Leg), whose value names the leg that ends at the entity addressed by the URI. Five values are defined, such as homea-homeb and visiteda-homea.
tldr.outcome: Networks can make decisions about things like media anchoring, signaling policy, transcoders and charging based on the leg type, as long as the parameter is trusted only inside a trust domain and operators have agreed to its use.

facts.label: Used in
facts.value: Request-URI, Route, Path and Service-Route URIs

today: RFC 7549 is a Proposed Standard from May 2015 and, according to the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its text says the parameter has known uses in 3GPP networks and that use in other networks is also possible.

sections.title: Why Traffic Legs Need Labels
sections.content:
In a 3GPP network, a user device can be attached to its own operator network (the home network) or to another operator's network (a visited network, when the user is roaming). Operator networks are often not connected directly, so there may be 3GPP transit networks in between that act at the SIP level or the IP level.

The signaling path between a calling user and a called user can be divided into segments called traffic legs. Each leg may span networks of different operators and can have its own characteristics. One leg may even involve several SIP dialogs, for example when a back-to-back user agent that changes the dialog identifier sits inside it.

Knowing the leg type helps intermediaries make policy decisions about media anchoring, signaling policy, insertion of media functions such as a transcoder, and charging.
sections.eli5: A message may travel through several networks before it arrives, like a parcel passing between delivery companies. Each stretch is a leg, and a label helps each company treat that stretch the right way.

sections.title: Traffic Leg Examples
sections.content:
The calling user (Alice) is attached to an originating network, which is either her home network or a visited network. Either way, her originating services come from her home network. The same holds for the called user (Bob) and the terminating network. A transit network, for example one that translates free phone numbers, may sit between the networks.

The RFC gives three examples of legs. In an originating roaming call, the leg between Alice's user agent and her home S-CSCF is the 'visiteda-homea' leg. In a terminating roaming call, the leg between Bob's home S-CSCF and Bob's user agent is the 'homeb-visitedb' leg. When the home S-CSCF of Alice forwards the initial INVITE to the home S-CSCF of Bob, that path is the 'homea-homeb' leg.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter that goes from your house to your home post office, then to your friend's post office, then to your friend's house. Each of those hops is a leg with its own name.

sections.title: How the Parameter Is Used
sections.content:
When a SIP entity puts a SIP URI into an initial request for a dialog, or into a stand-alone request, and the entity at that URI (or responsible for its host part) is the end of one or more traffic legs, the inserting entity can add an iotl parameter to that URI. The entity can put it in the Request-URI or in the URI of a Route header field. It can also add it to a Path or Service-Route header field so that it later shows up in a Route header field.

The receiver works out the leg type as follows. With a single Route header field containing an iotl parameter, that parameter counts. With several, the parameter on the topmost Route header field counts, or, if the topmost has none, the one closest to the top. If only the Request-URI has the parameter, that one counts.

During registration, entities can add the parameter to Path or Service-Route if they know the URI will mark the end of a specific leg for later requests. A SIP proxy must not modify or remove URI parameters on URIs that belong to other entities, and that applies to iotl. Entities that do not understand the parameter simply ignore it, as RFC 3261 defines.
sections.eli5: The sender sticks the label on the address it puts on the envelope. Whoever reads the address looks at the label closest to the top. Anyone who does not know what the label means just ignores it.

sections.title: The Five Parameter Values
sections.content:
RFC 7549 defines five values, each naming the two ends of a leg. In each case the text says what the leg is in 3GPP terms.

  • homea-homeb: between the originating home network and the terminating home network; in 3GPP, between two S-CSCFs.
  • homeb-visitedb: between the terminating home network and the visited network where the called user is; in 3GPP, between the home S-CSCF and the called user's UE, or between the SCC AS in the home network and the ATCF in the visited network.
  • visiteda-homea: between the visited network of the calling user and her home network; in 3GPP, between the UE and the home S-CSCF, or between the visited P-CSCF and the home S-CSCF.
  • homea-visiteda: between the originating home network and the visited network of the calling user; in 3GPP, between the calling user's home S-CSCF and the TRF serving her. It exists when the home S-CSCF forwards a request back to the visited network, for example when RAVEL is enabled.
  • visiteda-homeb: between the calling user's visited network and the called user's home network; in 3GPP, between the TRF serving the caller and the called user's home S-CSCF, for example when RAVEL is enabled.

When a request crosses between networks, it may pass one or more IBCFs (Interconnection Border Control Functions) acting as border entities.
sections.eli5: Each value is a name for one stretch of the trip, such as 'my house to my post office' or 'my post office to your post office'.

sections.title: Syntax and Registration
sections.content:
The grammar, in ABNF, allows one or two values separated by a dot: iotl-param = iotl-tag "=" iotl-value ["." iotl-value]. The tag is iotl. A value is one of the five defined names or an other-iotl, which is one or more letters, digits or hyphens. That open-ended form leaves room for future values.

The RFC creates no IANA registry for parameter values and says one should be considered if new values are defined later. IANA has added one entry, iotl (with predefined values), to the SIP/SIPS URI Parameters registry defined in RFC 3969.
sections.eli5: The label has a simple spelling rule: the word 'iotl', an equals sign, then a name made of letters, numbers and dashes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The parameter feeds policy decisions about charging and the triggering of services, so abuse could cause wrong user billing or service failure. To prevent that, the parameter SHOULD only be used for policy decisions by nodes in the same trust domain (see RFC 3325). Network boundary entities MUST NOT forward information received from untrusted entities. An agreement MUST also exist between the operators for use of the roaming role information.

General SIP security considerations are in RFC 3261.
sections.eli5: Because the label can change how much someone is charged, you should only trust labels from friends you have agreed with, and never pass on labels from strangers.

sections.title: Worked Call Flows
sections.content:
The appendix shows how the parameter travels. On registration, the visited P-CSCF adds iotl=homeb-visitedb to the Path header field, for later routing toward Alice. The home S-CSCF adds iotl=visiteda-homea to the Service-Route header field, for Alice's originating requests.

In an originating INVITE from Alice, the visiteda-homea value from Service-Route goes onto the Route header field for the S-CSCF. In a terminating INVITE toward Alice, the homeb-visitedb value from the Path header goes onto the Route header field for the P-CSCF. For a call between the two home networks, the originating S-CSCF puts iotl=homea-homeb in the Request-URI of the INVITE.
sections.eli5: When you sign up, each office hands you a label to use later. When you send a message, you copy the right label onto it.
